What does concord (subject-verb agreement) mean, and why does it matter for BECE?

Concord, also called agreement, means matching words correctly so a sentence sounds right. The most important type is subject-verb concord: the verb must agree with its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. For example, 'The boy runs' is singular, while 'The boys run' is plural. Notice the -s pattern is the opposite of nouns: it goes on the singular verb but the plural noun. Concord is one of the most tested areas in BECE and WAEC because errors are so common in everyday speech. Master it and you will write and speak far more correctly.

Choose the correct verb: The list of names (is/are) on the table.

The correct answer is 'is': 'The list of names is on the table.' Here is the reasoning.

Step 1: find the true subject of the sentence. It is 'the list', which is singular.
Step 2: ignore the words in between. 'Of names' is only a prepositional phrase describing the list; it does not change the subject.
Step 3: match the verb to the real subject, so singular 'list' takes singular 'is'. The plural noun 'names' sitting right before the verb is a trap examiners love. Whenever a phrase separates the subject from the verb, mentally remove it and the correct verb becomes clear.

Is it 'Everybody are' or 'Everybody is'?

The correct form is 'Everybody is'. Words like everybody, everyone, somebody, someone, nobody, anybody, each and either are called indefinite pronouns, and they are always singular, even though they seem to refer to many people. So we say 'Everybody is happy', 'Each of the students has a book', and 'Nobody was absent'. A helpful trick: these words often end in '-body' or '-one', and 'one' is clearly singular. In the market you might hear 'Everybody are here', but in writing and in exams it must be 'Everybody is here'. Learn this rule well, because it appears in almost every English paper.

What verb do I use with two subjects joined by 'and'?

When two subjects are joined by 'and', they form a plural subject and take a plural verb. For example, 'Bola and Musa are my friends', not 'is my friends'. The two people together make more than one, so the verb must be plural. But watch this special case: when the two joined words refer to a single thing or person, the verb stays singular, as in 'Rice and stew is my favourite meal' (one dish) or 'The head teacher and proprietor was present' (one person holding both roles). So the rule is: 'and' usually makes the subject plural, unless the joined words name one single unit. Read the meaning carefully before choosing the verb.

With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', which subject does the verb agree with?

With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject that is NEARER to it, not both. This is called the proximity rule. Look at the noun just before the verb and match the verb to it. Examples: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were ready' — 'students' is nearer, so the verb is plural 'were'. But 'Neither the students nor the teacher was ready' — now 'teacher' is nearer, so the verb is singular 'was'. The same works for 'either...or': 'Either Ada or her brothers are coming.' So before choosing the verb, find the subject closest to it, and let the verb agree with that one. Rearranging the sentence changes the verb.

Correct this sentence: The team of players were defeated.

The corrected sentence is: 'The team of players was defeated.' Here is why.

Step 1: identify the subject. It is 'the team', a collective noun treated here as one single unit, so it is singular.
Step 2: set aside the phrase 'of players', which merely describes the team and does not change the subject.
Step 3: match the verb to 'team', so it must be singular 'was', not plural 'were'. Collective nouns like team, family, class, committee and government usually take a singular verb when the group acts as one body. The plural 'players' next to the verb is the trap. Remove the middle phrase and 'The team was defeated' reads correctly.

Which is correct: 'Ten thousand naira is' or 'are' enough?

The correct form is 'Ten thousand naira is enough.' When an amount of money, a period of time, a distance or a weight is thought of as ONE whole quantity, it takes a singular verb, even though the number sounds plural. So we say 'Ten thousand naira is enough for the books', 'Five years is a long time', and 'Two kilometres is not far to trek.' We treat the whole amount as a single lump, not as separate units. The trick is to ask yourself: is this one total quantity? If yes, use a singular verb. This rule surprises many students because the big number makes them reach for a plural verb, but the meaning is what counts.

How do I check concord quickly in an exam?

Use this quick three-step check on any sentence.

Step 1: find the real subject by asking 'who or what is doing the action?' — and ignore any phrase that comes between the subject and the verb.
Step 2: decide whether that subject is singular or plural, remembering the special cases: everybody/each are singular; 'A and B' is usually plural; with either/or and neither/nor the verb follows the nearer subject; collective nouns and amounts of money or time are usually singular.
Step 3: make the verb agree. A fast test is to strip the sentence to its bare subject and verb, like turning 'The basket of mangoes is heavy' into 'The basket is heavy' — the correct verb becomes obvious.

Practise this and concord errors will disappear.
